events.title: The martyrdom of St. Valentine
events.shortBlurb: A Roman priest put to death for the faith on the Flaminian Way, whose name the fourteenth of February has borne ever since…
body: Ancient tradition holds that on 14 February, about the year 269, a priest named Valentine was martyred at Rome under the Emperor Claudius and buried on the Via Flaminia, where a basilica was later raised over his tomb. The Roman Martyrology still commemorates him on that day as a martyr who died on the Flaminian Way.

Of his life almost nothing is known with certainty. Later legends call him a priest of Rome or a bishop of Terni who restored sight to his judge's blind daughter and was beaten with clubs and beheaded for refusing to sacrifice, but the acts are late and unhistorical. In 1969 the Church removed his feast from the General Roman Calendar, while keeping his name among the martyrs.

The day's association with lovers is no part of his story. It arose in the later Middle Ages from the belief that birds paired in mid-February, a fancy Geoffrey Chaucer wove into his Parliament of Fowls, from which the customs of Valentine's Day descend. What the Church honors is simply a witness who gave his life for Christ.
